stories.headline: Trump halts Iran strikes, cites deal outline

claims.text: President Trump posted on Truth Social late Saturday.
Trump said he canceled planned U.S. strikes on Iran.
Trump cited a request from Iran and other Middle East countries for the cancellation.
Trump stated the 'perimeters of a deal' had been agreed to.
Trump said the U.S. was 'locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II'.
Trump agreed to cancel the attack 'subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL'.
Trump said Israel was part of that commitment.
Trump said the prospective deal would include the 'Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT'.
Trump said the deal would include an end to Iran's nuclear threat.
A statement carried by Saudi Arabia's state news agency (SPA) said Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke with Trump.
The SPA statement said Mohammed bin Salman emphasized prioritizing dialogue and de-escalation to prevent a wider conflict.
Iran's semi-official Mehr news agency, citing unnamed Iranian military officials, denied Iran had asked for a halt.
Mehr news agency reported that unnamed Iranian military officials called Trump's claim 'simply a new lie'.
Iran's acting Defense Minister Majid Ibn al-Reza said Tehran views all threats from adversaries as 'real and credible'.
U.S. media reports, including CBS News sourcing, indicated the U.S. and Israel had been preparing an intensified strike campaign on Iran's energy infrastructure.
The strike campaign plan was reportedly discussed at Trump's Friday cabinet meeting.
An AP poll this week found nearly two-thirds of Americans say the conflict with Iran is not worth the fight.
A Pew Research Center survey found about 60% of Americans disapprove of the war.
GOP Sen. James Lankford (Okla.) said on Fox News Sunday that Trump 'has no desire' to bomb Iran.
Sen. Lankford said Trump 'is still focused on trying to be able to get a deal'.

facts: President Trump posted on Truth Social late Saturday saying he canceled planned U.S. strikes on Iran, citing a request from Iran and other Middle East countries and stating the "perimeters of a deal" had been agreed to.

Trump said the U.S. was "locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II," but agreed to cancel the attack "subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL," adding that Israel was part of that commitment.
Trump said the prospective deal would include the "Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT" and an end to Iran's nuclear threat.

A statement carried by Saudi Arabia's state news agency (SPA) said Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke with Trump and emphasized prioritizing dialogue and de-escalation to prevent a wider conflict.

Iran's semi-official Mehr news agency, citing unnamed Iranian military officials, denied Iran had asked for a halt, calling Trump's claim "simply a new lie"; Iran's acting Defense Minister Majid Ibn al-Reza said Tehran views all threats from adversaries as "real and credible."

U.S. media reports, including CBS News sourcing, indicated the U.S. and Israel had been preparing an intensified strike campaign on Iran's energy infrastructure, a plan reportedly discussed at Trump's Friday cabinet meeting.
An AP poll this week found nearly two-thirds of Americans say the conflict with Iran is not worth the fight; a Pew Research Center survey found about 60% of Americans disapprove of the war.
GOP Sen. James Lankford (Okla.) said on Fox News Sunday that Trump "has no desire" to bomb Iran and "is still focused on trying to be able to get a deal."
ladder.analysis: The announcement caps months of escalation between the U.S./Israel and Iran that began with strikes in February and continued after an April ceasefire collapsed in June, involving U.S. blockades of Iranian ports, Iranian missile and drone attacks on U.S. assets, and repeated threats to the Strait of Hormuz, a critical global oil corridor. Trump's pattern of issuing severe military threats followed by diplomatic off-ramps has recurred before, including an April warning that "a whole civilisation will die tonight" that preceded talks in Pakistan which ultimately produced no agreement. Regional actors, particularly Saudi Arabia and Gulf states like Bahrain, Jordan and the UAE, have pushed for de-escalation because their infrastructure, unlike the U.S. mainland, is within range of Iranian retaliation.

dem: Some Democratic-aligned skeptics could point to Iran's flat denial that it requested a halt as evidence the administration's rationale for standing down is not fully verifiable, raising questions about transparency in how military decisions are being communicated to the public.

Given AP and Pew polling showing 60-65% of Americans view the conflict unfavorably, Democrats could argue the reversal reflects domestic political pressure and midterm considerations as much as diplomatic progress.
rep: Sen. James Lankford and other Trump allies frame the move as evidence the president never intended war for its own sake and is using maximum pressure to extract a negotiated deal, consistent with a strategy that previously produced direct US-Iran talks in Pakistan.

Supporters of the administration's approach argue that visible readiness to strike ("locked and loaded") combined with willingness to stand down on request from regional allies like Saudi Arabia demonstrates a coordinated, allies-informed strategy rather than unilateral escalation.

ladder.steelman: Regardless of political framing, the durability of any agreement is unproven: Iran has publicly denied requesting the halt and a prior round of high-profile talks in Pakistan ended without a deal, meaning both supporters and skeptics of Trump's approach are working from the same underlying uncertainty about whether this pause will hold.
ladder.implications: The immediate question is whether Iran and the U.S. can translate the announced "perimeters of a deal" into a finalized agreement covering Strait of Hormuz access and Iran's nuclear program before tensions reignite; Iran's public denial of requesting the pause suggests the diplomatic footing remains fragile. Continued uncertainty is likely to keep oil markets volatile, and with domestic polling showing majority disapproval of the conflict, the administration's handling of the situation could carry weight heading into the midterm elections.

stories.headline: Federal contract ends, leaving 25,000 immigrant children without legal representation

For more than two decades, federal law has required the U.S. government to provide protections for children who cross the border without a parent or guardian.
Unaccompanied children are transferred to the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR).
ORR had funded a Congress-appropriated network of nearly 100 legal groups to provide legal services to unaccompanied children.
The legal services network is managed by the nonprofit Acacia Center for Justice.
ORR stopped paying for these legal services in November.
Attorneys declined to provide ORR with confidential information about the children.
The lawyers say the confidential information is protected by attorney-client privilege.
The legal-services contract between ORR and the provider network expired Friday and was not renewed.
A group of legal nonprofits filed a lawsuit last year seeking a court order for the government to pay roughly $65 million owed.
The lawsuit also sought to continue funding services.
ProBAR, a project of the American Bar Association, laid off more than 20% of its staff.

facts: An estimated 25,000-26,000 unaccompanied migrant children are expected to lose independent legal representation as soon as Monday, according to lawyers who represent them.

For more than two decades, federal law has required the U.S. government to provide protections for children who cross the border without a parent or guardian, due to risks of exploitation, abuse, or trafficking.

Unaccompanied children are transferred to the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), which had funded a Congress-appropriated network of nearly 100 legal groups to provide them legal services, managed by the nonprofit Acacia Center for Justice.

ORR stopped paying for these legal services in November after attorneys declined to provide the agency with confidential information about the children, which the lawyers say is protected by attorney-client privilege.
The legal-services contract between ORR and the provider network expired Friday and was not renewed.
A group of legal nonprofits filed a lawsuit last year seeking a court order for the government to pay roughly $65 million owed and to continue funding services.

ProBAR, a project of the American Bar Association providing legal services to ORR-custody children, laid off more than 20% of its staff, according to a July 31 statement from its legal director, Lauren Fisher Flores.

On July 29, Acacia was notified that ORR was considering a new contract, possibly with different legal providers, but details were not shared; almost 1,800 children were in ORR custody as of June, with an average custody time of 194 days before release to sponsors under a 2008 law requiring prompt placement.
ladder.analysis: Unaccompanied immigrant children occupy a unique legal position: unlike criminal defendants, they have no guaranteed right to government-funded counsel in immigration proceedings, so the congressionally funded legal-services network has functioned as the primary safeguard ensuring they understand their rights and can contest deportation. The dispute stems from a standoff over confidential attorney-client information ORR sought from the legal providers, which the providers refused to hand over, leading ORR to withhold payment and ultimately let the contract lapse. This has produced both a funding crisis for legal nonprofits — forcing layoffs and reduced services — and a pending question of who, if anyone, will represent children in immigration court starting Monday, with the future of a replacement contract still undefined.

dem: Immigration attorneys and advocacy groups, as represented by Acacia Center for Justice and Alexa Sendukas of the Galveston-Houston Immigrant Representation Project, argue the government is improperly withholding payment for completed work to coerce lawyers into breaching attorney-client privilege, and that cutting off representation will lead to unrepresented children being deported, some into dangerous situations.

Legal service providers such as Immigrant Defenders Law Center frame their continued, unpaid appearance in court as an ethical obligation to children already in their care, implicitly criticizing the administration for creating a funding gap that forces attorneys to work without compensation.

Advocates point to the 2008 sponsor-placement law and the extended 194-day average custody time as evidence that ORR is already falling short of its obligations to children, arguing the contract lapse compounds an existing failure to protect this population.
rep: Because neither ORR nor the White House responded to NPR's requests for comment, the administration's specific rationale is not stated in this reporting; however, the underlying dispute centers on ORR's request for information about the children that it says it needs, which could be framed by supporters of stricter oversight as a legitimate accountability measure over federally funded contractors handling vulnerable minors.

Supporters of tighter immigration enforcement could note that ORR is reportedly considering awarding a new contract, potentially to different providers, suggesting the agency's position is that the process is a contracting and oversight matter rather than an attempt to end legal protections outright.

Some within this camp might argue that attorney-client privilege claims by contractors receiving federal funds do not exempt them from standard government reporting or auditing requirements tied to public funding, framing the standoff as a compliance dispute rather than a rights violation.

ladder.steelman: At root, this is a clash between the government's asserted right to information from federally funded contractors and attorneys' assertion of confidentiality obligations to their child clients — a procedural and legal dispute whose fallout, intended or not, is a near-total collapse of legal representation for tens of thousands of unaccompanied minors.
ladder.implications: With the contract lapsed and a replacement still undefined, thousands of children may face immigration court proceedings without legal representation as early as Monday, raising the likelihood of increased deportation orders for unaccompanied minors; the outcome of the pending lawsuit over unpaid funds, and clarity on any new ORR contract, will determine whether and how quickly legal services can be restored.

stories.headline: Trump slashes Medicare drug subsidies, cutting against affordability message

spectrum.tilt_pill: Coverage is balanced across the spectrum

claims.text: The Trump administration ended a subsidy program that had helped hold down costs for Medicare drug coverage.
The change could leave millions of Medicare enrollees facing higher monthly costs.
President Trump has publicly promoted lowering drug costs through a platform called TrumpRx.
Trump has also promoted pursuing 'most-favored-nation' drug pricing deals, under which the U.S. would pay prices comparable to other wealthy countries.

facts: The Trump administration ended a subsidy program that had helped hold down costs for Medicare drug coverage, according to The Hill.
The Hill reports the change could leave millions of Medicare enrollees facing higher monthly costs.
President Trump has publicly promoted lowering drug costs through a platform called TrumpRx.
Trump has also promoted pursuing 'most-favored-nation' drug pricing deals, under which the U.S. would pay prices comparable to other wealthy countries.
The Hill frames the subsidy cut as running counter to the administration's public messaging on drug affordability.
ladder.analysis: The story centers on an apparent tension within the Trump administration's health policy: while the White House publicly emphasizes lowering prescription drug costs through initiatives like TrumpRx and 'most-favored-nation' pricing deals, it has simultaneously ended a subsidy program that had helped keep Medicare drug coverage premiums or costs lower for enrollees. The source material does not specify the name of the subsidy program, the dollar amounts involved, an effective date, or the precise mechanism by which costs would rise, so those details cannot be verified from what's provided. The core, verifiable point is a reported contradiction between stated affordability goals and an administrative action that could raise out-of-pocket costs for seniors on Medicare drug plans.

dem: Democrats are likely to argue this shows the administration's affordability rhetoric is not matched by policy, since ending a cost-reducing subsidy directly raises what seniors pay out of pocket.
Democrats may contend that TrumpRx and most-favored-nation pricing are limited or symbolic gestures that don't offset the concrete, immediate cost increase from losing the subsidy.
rep: Republicans and the administration would likely argue that TrumpRx and most-favored-nation drug deals represent the real, structural fix to high drug prices, and that ending a specific subsidy is a separate budgetary or policy decision not in conflict with that broader goal.

Administration defenders may frame the subsidy's end as part of streamlining government spending, distinct from the price-lowering initiatives aimed at drugmakers rather than at Medicare premium supports.

ladder.steelman: The story's real tension is between two different tools for addressing drug costs — supply-side deals with manufacturers versus demand-side subsidies for consumers — and cutting one while touting the other can be simultaneously true and politically contradictory.
ladder.implications: If the subsidy's end takes effect, seniors enrolled in affected Medicare drug plans could see increased monthly costs in the near term, which may become a point of political attack regardless of any longer-term savings the administration expects from its pricing initiatives; further reporting would need to clarify the program's name, cost impact, and timeline to fully assess the scale of the effect.

claims.text: Wildfires have burned more than 250,000 acres in Washington state.
Thousands of residents have been evacuated because of the fires.
The fires caused power outages in the Spokane area.
Spokane is Washington's second most populous city.
Washington Governor Bob Ferguson declared a statewide emergency and a burn ban on Saturday morning.
Governor Ferguson said the state is facing 'a very serious situation with multiple fires'.
Governor Ferguson expressed sympathy for residents losing their homes.
Officials have reported no injuries or fatalities as of the report.

facts: Wildfires have burned more than 250,000 acres in Washington state, according to officials.
Thousands of residents have been evacuated because of the fires.
The fires caused power outages in the Spokane area, Washington's second most populous city.
Washington Governor Bob Ferguson declared a statewide emergency and a burn ban on Saturday morning.
Governor Ferguson said the state is facing 'a very serious situation with multiple fires' and expressed sympathy for residents losing their homes.
Officials have reported no injuries or fatalities as of the report.
ladder.analysis: This is a breaking natural-disaster story rather than a policy dispute: large wildfires in eastern Washington have prompted mass evacuations, power outages, and a statewide emergency declaration by Governor Bob Ferguson. A gubernatorial emergency declaration and burn ban are standard administrative tools that unlock state resources, mobilize firefighting personnel, and restrict activities (like open burning) that could spark new fires. The scale — over 250,000 acres — and the fact that the fires reached the edges of Spokane, the state's second-largest city, indicate the severity of the event, though the absence of reported injuries or deaths so far is a notable mitigating factor.
ladder.implications: Attention will likely turn to containment progress, the scale of property losses, and whether federal disaster assistance is requested as the fires continue to burn; the burn ban and emergency declaration give state officials expanded authority to respond in the coming days.

stories.headline: Trump halts strikes on Iran, says deal outline reached; US urges citizens to leave Middle East
body: US President Donald Trump said Saturday that he had canceled planned strikes on Iran after being asked by Iran and other Middle Eastern countries to hold off, claiming that the "perimeters of a deal" had been agreed to. In a social media post, Trump said the emerging agreement would include the "Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran's nuclear threat." He added that Israel had agreed to join the US in the commitment to pause strikes, subject to "being able to rapidly make a DEAL."

Iran quickly pushed back on Trump's characterization. Iran's Mehr news agency, citing military officials, called the claim that Tehran had asked the US not to strike "a new lie." Iran's acting Defence Minister, Brigadier General Majid Ebn-e-Reza, said Trump's pullback comment was made "within the context of psychological operations and a war of calculations" and that Iran's armed forces "will neither be taken by surprise nor will we be passive." Iran's wartime military command had warned Saturday that US and other interests across the region could be attacked in tit-for-tat strikes if Washington launched threatened attacks against civilian infrastructure.

The US State Department on Saturday issued a security alert urging Americans across the Middle East to "consider departing, or be prepared to depart should there be escalation." The alert warned that "US diplomatic facilities, including outside the Middle East, have been targeted" and that "Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other US interests overseas." US embassies in Bahrain, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates reposted the alert, warning of "unexpected escalation."

The announcement came amid reports that Trump could have ordered fresh strikes against Iran as soon as this weekend. US media quoted officials saying the US and Israel were planning one of the harshest bombing campaigns to date against energy infrastructure targets in Iran. At a cabinet meeting Friday, Trump was heard saying, "We'll be hitting them [Iranians] very hard. At some point, they're going to say, 'We just can't take it anymore.'" On Thursday, the US military said it had completed a "heavy wave" of strikes against IRGC targets in response to Iranian attacks on US bases and ships. Iranian state media said three people, including a two-year-old child, were killed in those strikes.

The conflict, which began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February, has escalated since a ceasefire in April fell apart in June. A memorandum of understanding reached that month partially reopened the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for lifting a US blockade on Iran's southern ports and a two-month relief from oil sanctions, but all provisions have since been rolled back. The IRGC has continued to strike or turn back ships attempting to use the strait. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke by phone with Trump before his announcement, stressing the need to prioritize dialogue to de-escalate tensions. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also spoke with his Saudi counterpart Saturday night. Other mediators including Pakistan, Qatar, Oman and Turkiye have been exchanging messages to nudge both sides toward an agreement.

In Tehran, some Iranians expressed skepticism. One resident told Al Jazeera she did not pay attention to the latest cycle of threats but was stressed that urban centers could be hit again. Iran's new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, who was selected in March after his father Ali Khamenei was killed in the opening salvo of the war, has not made any public appearance amid the ongoing battle over the Strait of Hormuz. A hardline member of parliament called for building underground "governance cities" to protect leaders from aerial bombardment. The UK Maritime Trade Operations reported two maritime incidents off Oman on Saturday, including one in which a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile, and Kuwait's army said it had detected and destroyed hostile drones targeting vital facilities.

stories.headline: EU holds emergency meeting as Ceuta migrant crisis death toll rises to 72
body: The European Union has called an emergency video conference of interior ministers for Tuesday after an estimated 50,000 to 60,000 migrants entered Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta over a three-day period, leaving at least 72 people dead. The bodies of the deceased were pulled from the sea, where they floated alongside abandoned rubber rings and flippers, according to Spanish authorities. Most of the migrants who crossed have since returned to Morocco, escorted by Spanish soldiers and police, and the situation in Ceuta has returned to near normal, Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said.

The influx, the largest ever recorded in Ceuta, began Wednesday and continued through Friday. Many migrants swam from Morocco using wetsuits and inflatables, bypassing the border fence by swimming around it or pushing through the wire. Ceuta’s top official, Juan Jesus Vivas, put the number of arrivals at about 60,000, while Spain’s Interior Ministry estimated 50,000. The enclave, which has a population of just 84,000, saw its reception centers overwhelmed, prompting calls for an emergency response. By Saturday, Grande-Marlaska said “almost all” migrants had left, and reinforced police and military deployments would remain as long as needed, though overnight crossings had fallen to nearly zero.

The emergency meeting was called after 22 of the EU’s 27 member states issued a joint letter calling for “coordinated action and the strengthening of external borders.” The letter stated, “We cannot allow uncontrolled mass crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration or other hybrid threats to create the perception that illegal entry into the European Union is possible. And, that a migrant’s illegal entry can turn into legal stay.” Italy suspended its Schengen open-border policy with Spain, a move Madrid condemned as politically motivated, noting that Ceuta is not in the Schengen zone and that the two countries do not share a land border. France announced a five-fold increase in police at its border with Spain, and Portugal said it would beef up controls at its southern land and maritime borders. Manfred Weber, leader of the European People’s Party, called for giving the European border agency Frontex “real enforcement powers” and said, “If a left-wing government in Spain is not willing to secure the external border, then Frontex must also be given command authority.”

The trigger for the mass crossing remains unclear. Spanish officials have pointed to a July 8 Supreme Court ruling that said migrants intercepted at sea cannot be summarily returned, though the ruling does not apply to land entries. Grande-Marlaska blamed people-smuggling networks for exploiting vulnerable migrants and spreading misleading interpretations of the ruling. Other experts questioned whether many migrants would have been aware of the court decision, suggesting instead that Spain’s relatively open migration policy—including a recent move to allow hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrants to apply for residence and work permits—may have played a role. Social media posts promising an easy path to Europe also circulated widely, with migrants showing reporters videos of people shouting “Spain is Open” and jumping into the sea. Multiple accounts, some only active for weeks, posted images of young people in wetsuits and flippers, amassing tens of thousands of likes. All such promises proved false; migrants who reached Ceuta found no food, shelter, or route to continental Europe, and most quickly turned back.

The crisis has exposed political divisions within Europe. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez criticized some EU members for “attacking” Spain instead of showing support, specifically targeting Italy’s hard-right Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who posted images of migrants in Ceuta with the caption, “This is the Sanchez model the Italian left wing likes so much.” Meloni faces elections next year and has been losing ground to a virulently anti-immigrant party. US President Donald Trump, who has an election looming, described the situation as a “catastrophe” and an “invasion.” Russia has also gloated over the crisis, which analysts say weakens Ukraine’s allies. Sanchez has not blamed Morocco, calling Rabat a “good ally,” but his critics accuse him of appeasement. Spain is extending the border fence out to sea with orange buoys and will patrol the jetty to deter future swimmers. The EU interior ministers’ meeting next week will discuss strengthening external borders, with populist right-wing voices emboldened. Meanwhile, travellers from Spain to Italy face random document checks for a few weeks.

Among the dead was Faten Ben Omar El Azizi, a Moroccan footballer whose family said her Schengen visa was approved the same day she died. Hundreds mourned her at her burial. The crisis has left lingering questions about whether the influx was spontaneous or deliberately orchestrated, with some observers drawing parallels to the weaponization of migration seen in Belarus. For now, the global right wing has been “hyperventilating with happiness,” as journalist Andrea Rizzi wrote in Spain’s El Pais newspaper, while dozens of young people who chased a vision they saw online are being sent back to Morocco in coffins.

stories.headline: Russian missile attack kills nine in Kyiv as Zelensky warns air defenses overwhelmed
body: A Russian missile and drone barrage struck Kyiv before dawn on Saturday, killing at least nine people and wounding more than 30, Ukrainian officials said. The attack included 35 missiles and 185 attack drones, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said only one of 27 ballistic missiles was intercepted because Ukraine is running out of Patriot air defense missiles — the only weapon capable of stopping such projectiles.

The bombardment hit five areas of the capital, setting fires and trapping residents in damaged buildings. The heaviest toll was in the Darnytskyi district, where seven people died and 14 were injured, including two children, Ukraine's state emergency service reported. In the Solomianskyi district, falling debris and a blaze partially destroyed a five-story apartment building; two people died and eight were injured, including two children. A police officer was among the dead. Lithuania's foreign ministry said its embassy in Kyiv sustained damage from nearby missile strikes.

Zelensky renewed his appeal for Western air defense supplies, writing on social media that "every package of ballistic missile interceptors saves the lives of our people" and that the shortage of interceptors "only encourages Russia to carry out such deadly strikes." The attack came two days after a separate Russian strike killed at least 10 people elsewhere in Ukraine and followed Zelensky's meeting with President Donald Trump in Washington, where he urged the U.S. to grant Ukraine a license to produce its own Patriot interceptors.

On Friday, Trump said the U.S. had not agreed to allow Ukraine to manufacture Patriot systems, calling it "a hard thing to give away that kind of technology" and expressing concern that Ukraine could someday use the missiles against the U.S. — though he acknowledged that was unlikely. Zelensky said he spoke by phone Friday with Vice President JD Vance and reiterated that air defense, particularly Patriot interceptors, remains a top priority.

Beyond Kyiv, a Russian airstrike killed one person and wounded 19 in the southern city of Kherson. Ukraine continued its own long-range campaign, with Zelensky saying Ukrainian drones struck three oil refineries in Russia's Bashkortostan region, roughly 1,000 miles from the front lines. Ukrainian drones also sank a sanctioned Russian container ship, the Yanina, in the Black Sea. Russia's state nuclear operator Rosatom, which owns the vessel's operating subsidiary, said all 17 crew members were rescued and that the ship was carrying only civilian goods, calling the attack "piracy and robbery."

stories.headline: Ukrainian drones strike Russian oil refineries and Wildberries warehouse, killing eight
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Ukrainian drones struck multiple oil refineries and a Wildberries e-commerce warehouse across Russia overnight, killing at least eight people, regional governors said on Saturday. Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed it hit an oil refinery in Saratov, the Engels airbase, and an oil depot in Kaluga Oblast, part of a campaign to degrade Russia’s war-fighting capability. In Samara Oblast, a Wildberries warehouse in Novosemeykino was set ablaze; the company lists drone components and body armor on its website, and its banking arm was sanctioned by the European Union in July.

The Saratov refinery processes about 7 million metric tons of crude oil annually and supports Russia’s military-industrial complex, according to the General Staff. Engels airbase houses Tu-95MS and Tu-160 strategic bombers used to launch missile attacks on Ukraine. Saratov Oblast Governor Roman Busargin said two people were killed in the strikes there. Separately, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian drones struck three oil refineries in Bashkortostan, nearly 1,600 km (994 miles) from Ukraine, and that a sanctioned Russian container ship, the Yanina, sank in the Black Sea after being hit by drones. Russia’s state nuclear energy company Rosatom claimed the ship carried civilian goods.

The strikes came as Russia unleashed a massive ballistic missile and drone attack on Kyiv overnight, killing at least nine people and wounding 33, Ukraine’s state emergency service reported. A five-story residential building in the Solomianskyi district was damaged, with two deaths and eight injuries including two children. In the Darnytskyi district seven people were killed and 14 injured. Zelenskyy said Ukraine shot down only one of 27 ballistic missiles because of air-defense shortages and appealed for more Patriot systems. In Kherson, a Russian airstrike killed one person and wounded five.

Other developments over the weekend included the International Atomic Energy Agency reporting that the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant lost off-site power for nearly two hours, the 23rd such incident since the full-scale invasion. In annexed Crimea, power cuts have forced residents to queue for hot meals; a local official in Massandra said her workers served roughly 200 people daily. Lithuania’s foreign ministry said its embassy in Kyiv was damaged by a Russian missile strike, with no injuries, and summoned the Russian embassy representative to protest. Lithuania’s foreign minister said that continued support for Ukraine and sanctions on Russia are needed to end the aggression.

stories.headline: Three killed in Moscow restaurant blast; mayor calls it 'brutal terrorist act'
body: At least three people were killed and 21 others injured Saturday evening when a homemade explosive device detonated at the entrance of an upscale Italian restaurant in central Moscow, Russian authorities said. The National Anti-Terrorist Committee reported that a woman carrying the bomb tried to enter the Balzi Rossi restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square but was stopped by a security guard. The device exploded, killing the woman, the guard, and a restaurant patron.

The blast occurred at approximately 8:00 p.m. local time (17:00 GMT) near one of Moscow's seven Stalin-era skyscrapers. The restaurant's website said the venue had been closed for a private event. The Kommersant daily newspaper cited sources as saying the bomb was intended to harm guests on the restaurant's summer terrace. Heavily armed law enforcement officers sealed off the area, and roads around the square were briefly closed. A nearby evening cycling event was canceled.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin described the explosion as a 'brutal terrorist act' in an online post on Sunday, adding that 'those responsible for this crime will certainly be found and face the punishment they deserve.' He did not identify any suspects. The Moscow Investigative Committee said the attack was still under investigation, and no one had publicly claimed responsibility as of early Sunday afternoon.

Russian officials have not commented on any possible link to the war in Ukraine. In recent years, several senior Russian military figures have been assassinated in and around Moscow, with the government blaming Kyiv for those attacks. The explosion came amid a wave of Ukrainian drone strikes deep inside Russia overnight, including an attack on an apartment block in the city of Engels that killed two people and a strike on a Wildberries warehouse in Samara Oblast. Russia's Defense Ministry reported over 100 Ukrainian strikes in the Belgorod Oblast, leaving 14 people injured, and claimed 635 Ukrainian drones were shot down overall.

The Balzi Rossi restaurant apologized on social media for an initial post that said everything was safe on the premises, calling it 'highly inappropriate given the circumstances.' The restaurant said staff were focused on assisting guests and emergency services. State news agency RIA Novosti released video showing armed law enforcement officers at the cordoned-off scene.

stories.headline: Trump Calls Off Iran Strikes; Gulf Stocks Rise on De-escalation Hopes
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Gulf stocks rose, with de-escalation hopes and corporate earnings lifting sentiment, according to Reuters. Investor's Business Daily, in its futures coverage, said President Trump had called off Iran strikes, shifting market attention to how equities would react next.

The market was being pulled in two directions: investors were looking for signs of progress toward a US-Iran ceasefire deal, while also evaluating President Trump's progressively heated threats of escalation should Iran fail to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters described Iran headlines as pulling markets two ways, with escalation threats clashing with ceasefire talk.

The Strait of Hormuz is a strategically important waterway for global oil shipments, which gave the threat of closure outsized importance for markets. The apparent cancellation of strikes reduced the immediate risk of a broader conflict, helping Gulf stocks advance.

What happens next may hinge on official confirmation from Washington and on whether Iran moves to reopen the strait. Any shift between diplomacy and renewed military pressure is likely to drive the next market move.

stories.headline: S&P 500 Earnings Growth Accelerates, Over 80% Beat Estimates
body: S&P 500 earnings growth accelerated this week as more than 155 companies reported across key sectors, with 84% of those firms topping earnings-per-share estimates and 72% posting year-over-year profit growth, according to Seeking Alpha’s Earnings Scoreboard. The strong results were headlined by several of the so-called 'Magnificent Seven' mega-cap technology stocks, including Microsoft (MSFT), Apple (AAPL), Meta Platforms (META), and Amazon (AMZN), alongside chip makers.

Amazon was the latest Big Tech company to report abnormally large earnings growth, driven in part by paper gains on its investments in Anthropic, according to MarketWatch. Microsoft and Amazon notably outperformed with strong revenue and EPS growth fueled by cloud and AI demand, while Apple and Meta disappointed on some growth drivers and profitability, Seeking Alpha noted.

Most S&P 500 companies beat earnings and revenue estimates, with strong year-over-year growth seen in both metrics across multiple sectors. Seeking Alpha’s Quick Insights highlighted that investors should focus on consumer discretionary, healthcare, technology, industrials, energy, and real estate sectors going forward.

Major reports still expected include McDonald's, Eli Lilly, Palantir, and Caterpillar, according to Seeking Alpha. The continued acceleration in profit growth and the high beat rate underscore the resilience of corporate earnings amid shifting economic conditions.

stories.headline: Dodgers acquire two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal in blockbuster trade with Tigers
body: The Los Angeles Dodgers acquired two-time reigning American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal from the Detroit Tigers late Saturday night in a blockbuster trade ahead of the Aug. 3 trade deadline. The back-to-back defending World Series champions added the top starting pitcher available on the market, a rental who is set to become a free agent after the season. The move solidifies the Dodgers' bid for a third consecutive title, a feat not accomplished since the 1998–2000 New York Yankees.

In exchange, the Dodgers sent three prospects to Detroit: outfielder Zyhir Hope, right-hander River Ryan, and catcher Brady Smith. Hope, considered the headlining prospect in the deal, was originally acquired by the Dodgers from the Chicago Cubs in January 2024 as part of the trade for first baseman Michael Busch and reliever Yency Almonte. Ryan had come to the Dodgers from the San Diego Padres in an earlier deal, and Smith was a third-round pick in the 2023 draft. The connection to the Cubs was highlighted by The Athletic's Jim Bowden, who wrote: 'So the Dodgers acquired Zyhir Hope from the Cubs for Michael Busch and River Ryan from the Padres for Meatt Beatty and drafted Brady Smith in the 3rd round of '23 and turned them into Tarik Skubal. Got it.' Hope has pushed for a roster spot after a monster July in the minors, batting .372 with 10 home runs, six steals and a 1.184 OPS.

The trade was widely anticipated, as the Dodgers possess the prospect depth and financial resources to make such moves without crippling their long-term outlook. Skubal joins a rotation that already includes Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tyler Glasnow, and Blake Snell, with Shohei Ohtani sidelined from pitching due to a balky knee. Over his past six starts, Skubal posted a 1.95 ERA, 0.78 WHIP and 12.2 strikeouts per nine innings. CBS Sports’ Scott White had predicted the outcome, noting that the Dodgers are 'the organization that's landed every top prize of the past few years, the one with farm system that never seems to run out and the financial firepower to make homegrown talent entirely optional.' The trade leaves the Dodgers poised to enter the postseason with a rotation of Yamamoto, Skubal, Glasnow and Snell once the latter two return from injury.

The Tigers, now in rebuilding mode, restock their system with three prospects, including Hope, who is expected to be ready for the majors next season, and Ryan, who is recovering from a hamstring strain but likely to make his debut for Detroit later this season. With Skubal moved, Detroit may now deal other rental starters such as Casey Mize, who has been scratched from a start to protect his trade value. For the rest of the league, the move underscores the competitive imbalance in baseball, as only the Dodgers could afford to part with top prospects for a rental without significant long-term pain. Other contenders now turn to remaining available starters, including Angels' Reid Detmers, Mets' Clay Holmes and Freddy Peralta, Blue Jays' Kevin Gausman and Shane Bieber, and Giants' Robbie Ray.

stories.headline: Former IOC marketing chief: Infantino's leadership 'radioactive,' reign 'over' after FIFA investment plan backlash
body: FIFA president Gianni Infantino's leadership has become "radioactive" and his 10-year reign as head of world football "is over," according to Michael Payne, former head of marketing at the International Olympic Committee. Payne's comments to AFP come after a leaked FIFA plan to raise up to $4.2 billion through private investment — based on a $20 billion valuation of a new commercial subsidiary called the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) — sparked a furious global reaction, leading Infantino to shelve the scheme on Saturday.

The proposed FFE was intended to run events such as the World Cup and Club World Cup and included one-time payments of $20 million to each of FIFA's 211 member associations, who each hold one vote. The plan, which Payne described as a result of "gross hubris," quickly drew opposition from major football confederations. European governing body UEFA said it had lost "confidence" in Infantino over what it called a "shabby deal," while CONCACAF — which includes the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, the three recent co-hosts of the World Cup — called for "a comprehensive reckoning with this presidency."

"I do not think we have ever seen such a fast fall from grace by a sports leader," said Payne, who helped modernize the IOC's brand and finances over nearly two decades. "One week ago, Infantino was riding high from delivering a very successful World Cup, and expected to run unopposed for election next year to continue his mandate as president of FIFA. Now Infantino will struggle to survive the month." Payne added, "I don't see how any amount of lobbying or 'persuasion' of the smaller countries can save him. His leadership has become radioactive, and if he stays there will be total civil war in global football, with breakaways by leading nations and boycotts. It's over."

Terrence Burns, a brand and marketing strategist who worked on two successful World Cup hosting bids, told AFP he had never seen "anything mismanaged and bungled so badly by people so smart." Burns said Infantino's position is "precarious" but not beyond repair, noting that in FIFA elections, confederations do not vote as a bloc. "It's the individual associations that receive development money from Zurich," he said. Burns identified Africa (CAF) and Oceania as potentially pivotal: "If CAF stays with him, he can lose Europe, Asia, and CONCACAF in public and still win in the hall. If CAF moves, it's game over."

Burns added that Infantino has lost "inevitability" — a key asset that kept him unopposed in 2019 and 2023. "I think that calculation changed this week, before the 18 November nomination deadline," he said. Meanwhile, UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin emerged as a winner, according to Burns: "He played it well. UEFA carried the fight collectively while he issued no personal statement at any point, which means he can now stand, or not stand, for the FIFA presidency without having spent anything on the argument. The boycott threat was aggressive and credible, which is a rare pairing."

stories.headline: Josh Kerr wins Commonwealth Games mile gold in Glasgow, then spends 45 minutes with fans
body: Josh Kerr won the men's mile at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow on Saturday night, crossing the line in 3 minutes 54.12 seconds at Scotstoun Stadium. The 28-year-old Scot, who set a world record of 3:42.66 in London last month, held off Australian prodigy Cam Myers (silver) and former Olympic silver medallist Timothy Cheruiyot (bronze). His childhood friend and Scotland teammate Jake Wightman finished sixth.

The race was a physical, slow-paced affair with no pacers or wave lights. Kerr, who had emerged from fireworks spinning a bottle and allowed his rivals to sprint away before starting, was trapped in the pack for three laps. At the bell he burst to the outside, passed Myers and Cheruiyot with 250 metres to go, and celebrated by conducting the crowd during his final strides before wrapping himself in a Saltire.

After the medal ceremony, Kerr spent about 45 minutes taking selfies and signing autographs for fans. "I'm just trying to create a moment for them," he told BBC Sport Scotland. "There is absolutely nothing stopping any of them going out and doing what I've just done. I believe if you grow up in Scotland, you can be one of the best runners in the history of these distances." He added: "You've got to stay in your lane and realise I'm lucky coming into this championship healthy, ready to go and I'm in the best shape of my life. And to do that in front of a home crowd is very special."

Kerr, who grew up in Edinburgh and now lives in Albuquerque, New Mexico, said the Games meant "everything" to him. During the playing of Flower of Scotland on the podium, he repeatedly stopped singing to compose himself and wiped tears from his eyes. "To have Flower of Scotland playing versus the GB national anthem, it's just different," he said. "Not many times in my career I'll ever have that." He recalled watching the athletics at Hampden Park during the 2014 Commonwealth Games as a child, and said he wanted to inspire young Scots the way Sir Chris Hoy inspired him when Hoy spoke at his school assemblies.

Kerr had been candid about his goals for the summer: breaking the 27-year-old world record and winning Commonwealth gold. "This whole experience has been really fun for me," he said. "The city is buzzing with the Games and it's just nice to be a part of that and really feed off the city." Asked about being considered a sporting standard bearer for Scotland alongside Hoy and Sir Andy Murray, Kerr said: "It's an honour to be spoken in the same sentence as those two legends. I've got a lot of work to do to keep up with them."

stories.headline: Sharp Acceleration in Global Warming Detected by Scientists
body: Global warming has shifted into a faster gear, with the planet warming at about 0.35°C per decade over the past ten years compared to just under 0.2°C per decade from 1970 to 2015, according to a new analysis from the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK). The acceleration, visible around 2013–2015, appears in all five major global temperature datasets with a statistical certainty exceeding 98%, the researchers report in Geophysical Research Letters.

To isolate the long-term warming signal, scientists filtered out short-term natural influences such as El Niño events, volcanic eruptions, and solar cycles. "We can now demonstrate a strong and statistically significant acceleration of global warming since around 2015," said co-author Grant Foster, a U.S. statistics expert. After removing these factors, 2023 and 2024 remained the two warmest years since instrumental records began.

The study analyzed measurements from five widely used temperature datasets—NASA, NOAA, HadCRUT, Berkeley Earth, and ERA5—using two distinct statistical approaches: a quadratic trend analysis and a piecewise linear model. Both methods independently confirmed the acceleration. "The adjusted data show an acceleration of global warming since 2015 with a statistical certainty of over 98 percent, consistent across all data sets examined and independent of the analysis method chosen," said lead author Stefan Rahmstorf of PIK.

The research was designed to detect and measure the acceleration, not to identify its cause, but the authors noted that the observed speed-up is consistent with the range of behavior produced by current climate models. Rahmstorf warned that if the recent warming rate continues, it would lead to a long-term exceedance of the 1.5°C limit of the Paris Agreement before 2030. "How quickly the Earth continues to warm ultimately depends on how rapidly we reduce global CO2 emissions from fossil fuels to zero," he said.

stories.headline: Cyclospora Outbreak: How Parasite Infects Gut and Nurses Trace Sources
body: This summer, the United States is experiencing its largest recorded outbreak of cyclosporiasis, the disease caused by the Cyclospora parasite. As of a July 28 update from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 45 states have reported cases, with Michigan serving as the epicenter. More than 10,000 people in Michigan have been sickened, including over 900 in Washtenaw County alone, where public health nurses have conducted hundreds of interviews with patients. The outbreak has been linked to lettuce from Taylor Farms in central Mexico, which was voluntarily recalled on July 17, and health officials are also investigating parsley and cilantro as potential sources in North Carolina.

Cyclospora parasites are microscopic single-celled organisms that rely exclusively on the human gut to reproduce. They are transmitted via oocysts—pods about the size of a hundred linked end-to-end across a pinhead—that contaminate food or water. Once ingested, the oocysts travel to the small intestine, where signals like body temperature and bile trigger the release of parasites. The parasites burrow into intestinal cells, replicating from a few to millions, and eventually differentiate into egg- and sperm-like forms that combine to create new oocysts—a process that can occur millions of times during an infection. This destruction of intestinal cells reduces nutrient absorption, causing symptoms such as nausea and diarrhea. A single milliliter of diarrhea can contain around a thousand oocysts. The oocysts are shed in feces but are not immediately infectious; they must mature in the environment for days or weeks, surviving chlorine, sunlight, and cold. The hardiness of the oocysts and their ability to enter the food system through tainted water, soil, or unwashed hands contribute to the difficulty of controlling outbreaks.

Cyclosporiasis infections can last for weeks or months, far longer than typical viral stomach bugs. A combination of antibiotics (sold as Bactrim, Septra, or Cotrim) can stop the parasites from replicating, allowing the immune system to clear the infection. While the disease is rarely fatal, immunity can build over time: in regions where Cyclospora is endemic, older people tend to have fewer symptomatic infections. Scientists are puzzled about why the U.S. is seeing such a large outbreak this year. Dr. Bobbi Pritt, a microbiologist at the Mayo Clinic, noted that the imported food supply from endemic countries with poor sanitation is a major factor, but she added that the scale might be due to "bad luck" with a large dose contaminating a widely consumed product. Joel Barratt, a molecular parasitologist at Emory University, described the case numbers as "just going straight through the roof" after previous outbreaks in 2018 and 2019.

In Washtenaw County, public health nurse Linda Kim has been on the front lines of the outbreak response, conducting detailed interviews with sickened residents. Many patients describe the illness as excruciating, with some reporting graphic symptoms such as "pooping their beds." The interviews are complex because symptoms can take up to two weeks to appear, making it difficult for patients to recall what they ate. Kim asks patients to provide grocery store receipts, restaurant records, and app purchase histories, even inquiring about specific details like whether a taco was crunchy or soft. The health department's work has been hampered by federal funding cuts: the Trump administration's elimination of public health grants left Washtenaw County without a contract that funded 123 full-time employees across the state. While some funding was restored after a court order, the department has scaled back disease surveillance and outbreak response, and a CDC employee stationed there was fired, rehired, then furloughed. "It took them forever to say that this was lettuce," said nursing supervisor Christina Zilke, referring to the federal response. Health officials recommend washing and cooking fresh vegetables to reduce the risk of infection, and tracing efforts continue as authorities work to identify additional sources.

stories.headline: FDA Set to Decide on Moderna mRNA Flu Shot Amid Industry Skepticism and HHS Funding Cuts
body: The Food and Drug Administration faces a Wednesday deadline to decide whether to approve Moderna’s experimental mRNA-based flu shot, a decision that carries significant implications for the future of mRNA research. The agency’s deliberations come amid skepticism from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has long questioned the value of mRNA vaccine technology, and after the Department of Health and Human Services canceled nearly $500 million in mRNA vaccine research funding last summer.

Moderna’s application faced an unusual setback in February, when the FDA sent a letter refusing to review the submission. Stephen Hoge, Moderna’s president, described the moment as a shock, saying the company had consulted with the FDA at every step and had been told it could proceed. After a public outcry and a promise from Moderna to add a confirmatory study if the vaccine reaches the market, the FDA reversed course and agreed to review the application. In June, a panel of FDA advisers recommended approval.

If approved, the Moderna vaccine would be the first mRNA-based flu shot to reach the market. But the agency’s initial flip-flop has already had a chilling effect on the industry. Rena Conti, a health economist at Boston University, said investors depend on the FDA to be consistent and fair. “They don’t want to spend money if they don’t think there’s going to be a way to actually make money on the other end,” she said.

The HHS funding cuts and the FDA’s actions have also spooked venture capital firms that back smaller biotech companies working on mRNA therapies for conditions such as Lyme disease and rare cancers, according to Jeff Coller, a professor at Johns Hopkins University who has studied mRNA technology for decades. “When you see the FDA rejecting a product that comes from Moderna, why is it that my little company would be able to push through?” he said. Moderna’s president said the company is holding off on some planned mRNA research until it sees how the regulatory landscape settles.

The stakes for mRNA research extend beyond flu vaccines. Janusz Racz, a 69-year-old retired computer scientist in London, received an mRNA vaccine made by BioNTech in a clinical trial for Stage 3 lung cancer. After a year of regular vaccinations, the cancer is gone. Racz, a U.S. citizen, said he wrote a letter to Health Secretary Kennedy sharing his story and warning that cuts to mRNA research “cut off the hope” for millions of people. He said Kennedy never responded.

In response to NPR’s questions, an HHS spokesman provided a statement: “Under Secretary Kennedy’s leadership, HHS is advancing President Trump’s commitment to strengthen public health through gold-standard science, and FDA will continue applying rigorous, evidence-based standards to every product it reviews while supporting innovation that meets those standards.” The FDA’s decision on the Moderna flu shot is expected by Wednesday.

stories.headline: Study Links Cancer's Intense Gene Activity to Self-Induced DNA Damage
body: New research from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem suggests that cancer cells may damage their own DNA by forcing critical genes to operate at extreme levels. In a study released August 2, 2026, in Science Advances, investigators led by PhD student Osama Hidmi under Prof. Rami Aqeilan found that powerful DNA control regions called super-enhancers drive unusually intense activity in growth-related genes, placing physical strain on the DNA and leading to breaks. The damage is repeatedly repaired, but each repair cycle can introduce small errors, allowing mutations to accumulate and potentially helping tumors evolve and become more aggressive.

To multiply rapidly, cancer cells activate certain genes far more strongly than healthy cells normally would. Many of these genes help tumors divide, survive, and maintain cellular programs needed for continued growth. The researchers used a sensitive genome-mapping method to create detailed maps of double-strand breaks, among the most severe forms of DNA damage because both strands of the DNA molecule are severed. The breaks did not appear randomly; they clustered inside genes controlled by super-enhancers, sections of DNA that act as powerful control panels and keep cancer-promoting programs running at very high levels.

The team also followed a natural cellular alarm signal that marks damaged DNA and attracts repair machinery. Their results showed that cancer cells repeatedly damage and restore DNA within these intensely active regions. Repair allows tumor cells to survive, but every repair creates an opportunity for mistakes, and over time those mistakes may make the affected regions more likely to collect additional mutations. The findings suggest genetic instability may not simply be a side effect of cancer; it could emerge directly from the intense gene activity tumors require to keep growing. As mutations build up, cancer cells can develop traits that help them spread, withstand stressful conditions, or become less responsive to treatment.

"Cancer cells rely on super-enhancers to keep growth genes running at high speed," said Prof. Rami Aqeilan. "What we found is that this same high-output activity can put real strain on the DNA, creating break hotspots that the cell has to repair again and again. That cycle may help tumors survive in the short term, but it also increases the risk of mutations that can fuel cancer's evolution."

The same dependence may also create a vulnerability. "Because cancer cells depend on these high-stress DNA regions to keep growing, they may also be more vulnerable there," Hidmi said. "This opens the door to treatments that target the very processes tumors rely on to survive." Therapies might eventually be designed to disrupt the intense gene activity driven by super-enhancers or to prevent tumor cells from repairing the resulting DNA damage, making it harder for tumors to survive and continue evolving.

DNA damage and repair play major roles in how cancers grow, change, and resist treatment. The new study offers an explanation for where some of that damage occurs and what may be causing it, identifying cancer's strongest gene-control regions as possible weak points. The study, "Superenhancers shape the landscape and repair dynamics of transcription-associated DNA breaks in cancer," was published in Science Advances, Vol. 12, No. 4, with DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeb6379, from materials provided by the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

stories.headline: US-China AI race intensifies as American lead erodes, analysis warns
body: The United States' lead over China in artificial intelligence has all but vanished, according to a new analysis published by CNBC, which argues that Washington is increasingly reacting to Chinese breakthroughs rather than shaping the competitive environment. The analysis, written by Dewardric McNeal, managing director and senior policy analyst at Longview Global, contends that the defining question is no longer whether China can compete at the technological frontier, but whether the U.S. can adapt quickly enough to compete against a Chinese innovation ecosystem advancing on model performance, cost, deployment, customization, financing, standards, developer adoption, and global reach.

McNeal points to a series of Chinese AI firms—including DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, Alibaba's Qwen family of models, Tencent's Hunyuan, Zhipu AI, and MiniMax—as evidence that China has cultivated a frontier AI ecosystem capable of repeatedly producing world-class capabilities across multiple firms. He argues that these advances, whether emerging through original innovation, engineering optimization, open-weight collaboration, or distillation of U.S. models, collectively demonstrate a broader structural transformation rather than isolated events. The analysis notes that the U.S. has consistently underestimated China's long-term commitment to technological advancement, citing similar patterns in rare earths, electric vehicles, robotics, and semiconductors.

The piece introduces the concept of 'ecosystem statecraft,' describing it as a form of strategic competition that integrates industrial policy, finance, innovation, global standards, university curriculum direction, state-supported developer ecosystems, diplomacy, and commercial expansion into a coherent national strategy. McNeal argues that China's approach, articulated through industrial policies and Five-Year Plans for more than a decade, is now producing measurable results, with DeepSeek's January 2025 announcement serving as evidence that the strategy is beginning to succeed. He contrasts this with the U.S. approach, which he says has emphasized preserving technological leadership through frontier innovation and export controls, while Beijing focuses on shaping the ecosystem within which global technology competition occurs.

The analysis highlights a race to 'addict' the rest of the world to a tech stack, a phrase attributed to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during debate over an Nvidia chip export ban. McNeal warns that it is increasingly unclear that the American stack is the one gaining adoption, noting that Chinese AI firms are making their technologies easier to deploy, customize, and integrate across multiple computing environments. He argues that reducing friction throughout the technology stack may prove as important as improving benchmark performance, and that persuading countries to avoid Chinese AI will be more difficult than earlier campaigns against Huawei and ZTE, as technology adoption now occurs from the bottom up as much as from the top down.

McNeal cautions that many governments now evaluate both Washington and Beijing through a pragmatic lens, balancing security concerns with affordability, financing, technological capability, local capacity building, and long-term economic opportunity. He states that trust, financing, developer communities, standards, commercial partnerships, and diplomatic credibility have become competitive advantages. The analysis expresses concern that America's AI conversation is too often framed around the competitive interests of individual companies rather than the nation's long-term strategic interests, emphasizing that governments must optimize for national advantage, not just market advantage.

Despite these warnings, McNeal acknowledges that the U.S. retains extraordinary advantages, including unparalleled universities, a unmatched venture capital ecosystem, a semiconductor industry underpinning the global AI economy, and frontier laboratories producing extraordinary breakthroughs. However, he concludes that technological leadership is rarely determined solely by who invents it first, but by who builds the ecosystem that everyone else chooses to join. The question for the U.S., he writes, is whether it can develop a coherent national strategy combining technological innovation with trusted alliances, standards-setting, research, talent development, commercial partnerships, financing, and renewed international credibility—one capable of surviving changes in administrations.

stories.headline: Google DeepMind unveils Gemini Robotics 2 with full body control
body: Google DeepMind last week unveiled Gemini Robotics 2, the latest version of its vision-language-action (VLA) model, introducing intelligent whole-body control, advanced dexterity, and multi-robot collaboration. The updated model enables robots to reason through every movement, allowing a humanoid to walk, crouch, stretch, and manipulate objects to clean a cluttered room, and to team up with other robots to finish tasks faster. DeepMind also released Gemini Robotics ER 2, an embodied reasoning model that acts as an agent for communication and multi-step planning, and Gemini Robotics On-Device 2, a VLA optimized to run locally on robotic devices with fast adaptation to new robot embodiments using a few hours of data.

Gemini Robotics 2 expands physical AI from upper-body tabletop tasks to whole-body motions. When controlling Apptronik's Apollo 2 humanoid, the model processes an instruction such as 'put the watering can into the green bin on the bottom shelf,' then walks, picks up the can, steps to the shelves, and places it precisely. DeepMind noted that movement speed still needs improvement but called this an important step toward real-world tasks requiring whole-body coordination. The model also unlocks new dexterity across different end effectors: on the Apollo 2, it controls a five-fingered, 22-degree-of-freedom SharpaWave hand to tie knots or seal a ziplock bag, and on a Franka Duo platform it operates standard two-fingered parallel grippers for complex tasks like tight packing.

To manage complex multi-step tasks, Gemini Robotics ER 2 serves as the robot's high-level brain, processing user instructions, observing the room, reasoning about steps, coordinating with the VLA, and tracking progress. DeepMind said the update enables robots to reliably execute longer task sequences lasting several minutes and involving hundreds of decisions, with improved understanding of when tasks begin and end. The company also introduced multi-robot collaboration, allowing different types of robots to communicate and work together on workflows a single robot could not handle alone. Gemini Robotics ER 2 is now available on Google AI Studio and in private preview on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform; the VLA and On-Device models are available to early-access partners.

Gemini Robotics On-Device 2 is designed for applications with low connectivity, operating without network latency or internet. The model is natively multi-embodiment and inherits motion transfer techniques from Gemini Robotics 1.5. DeepMind claimed it can adapt to new bi-arm robot embodiments with just a few hours of adaptation time, typically using fewer than 200 examples, even for embodiments with drastically different shapes, sensors, and degrees of freedom.

DeepMind reaffirmed its commitment to safety, stating that Gemini Robotics 2 advances safety for navigating real-world uncertainty and collaborating alongside humans. The company introduced ASIMOV-Agentic, a new benchmark for agentic safety orchestration and uncertainty resolution that measures an embodied reasoning agent's ability to refuse unsafe tool calls from a VLA and to predict whether a task is possible, proactively requesting human intervention when uncertain. DeepMind said Gemini Robotics ER 2 is its safest robotics model to date in safety constraint following and human proximity benchmarks, capable of detecting when humans are nearby, triggering safety tool calls, and bringing the robot to a safe stop if someone approaches too closely—a key requirement in collaborative safety standards.

stories.headline: Australian booksellers condemn 'horrific' destruction of rare titles to feed AI training data
body: Booksellers at Melbourne's Rare Book Fair have spoken out against what they call the 'horrific' destruction of rare titles by generative AI companies, after a US copyright lawsuit revealed Anthropic engaged in 'destructive scanning' — buying physical books, slicing off spines for efficient scanning, then pulping the remains. The practice, ruled lawful under US copyright law as 'transformative use', is now understood to be widespread across the AI industry.

Multiple Australian secondhand booksellers told Guardian Australia they recently received unusual orders from a Canadian company called Zoom Books, a self-described book recycler. The orders came through large marketplaces like Abebooks and Biblio, and were price-insensitive, random, and involved niche titles — sometimes decades-old stock. Delfina Manor of Good Reading Secondhand Books in Benalla, Victoria, said she received orders amounting to three full boxes in May. John Sainsbury, owner of Melbourne's Sainsburys Books, confirmed a slew of such orders, including a 1970s manual on soil mechanics alongside a 2010 book on New Zealand cycling and a collection of early Australian poetry that sold for $9 after sitting on the shelf for 20 years.

Vendors suspect the books may be used for AI training data. Tim White, who runs independent bookshop Books for Cooks, said that while he would not mourn a common copy, 'if it's a book that has that storytelling element to it, or it's a one-off, it's horrific.' Rare bookseller Gwenyth Todd from Chatelaine Books said she screens buyers to keep books from going 'to the wrong home,' adding, 'To me books are more than just objects.' Not all sellers were entirely opposed: Nick Dawes of Grant's Bookshop, who estimates he has 500,000 books in his warehouses, said he would be ambivalent about a bulk sale but would draw the line at a unique copy.

An Anthropic spokesperson said the company has never bought from Zoom Books, but acknowledged 'sourcing books is a widely used approach for training large language models across the AI industry.' Anthropic said it procures books from mainstream commercial markets and does not 'buy and destroy rare or antiquarian books.' Zoom Books co-founder Manroop Gill posted on LinkedIn that the company had been 'expanding aggressively,' and a company spokesperson told Guardian Australia: 'We acquire secondhand books and resell them intact. We do not digitize books.' The company declined to disclose whether it sells intact books to AI companies, citing confidentiality agreements.
